title: Carol Countdown 2026: The Festive Four need your votes
summary: It’s March Madness in a Christmas sweater. “Joy to the World,” “Carol of the Bells,” “Silent Night” and “O Holy Night” are still standing. Your vote decides who makes the championship.
content: Alyssa Gonzalez/CPR Roll the tape, Shipmates! It’s March Madness in a Christmas sweater, and this is CPR Classical’s 2026 Carol Countdown: The Festive Four. [Cue SportsCenter-style music — da-da-dun, da-da-dun.] Every bracket needs a Cinderella, and ours came with wings: “Angels We Have Heard on High” pulled off an upset over “White Christmas” in Round 2. The crowd went wild. Bing Crosby demanded a replay. Then the Angels ran into “Carol of the Bells.” The Bells knocked them out 59.2% to 40.8% in the closest contest of the quarterfinals. Tough day for a team that showed up with its own wings. Cinderella’s going home, my friend. Elsewhere in the bracket, “Joy to the World” got past “The First Noel,” 62.8% to 37.2%, and “O Holy Night” topped “Coventry Carol,” 62.1% to 37.9%. And the loudest score in the building? That came from “Silent Night.” It sent “Winter Wonderland” a-packin’ 64.1% to 35.9% — the widest margin of the round. So much for home-ice advantage. Four heavyweights. Two tickets to the championship. You get to decide who wins. Get off the bench, Shipmate, and vote for your favorites today! I’m Kabin Thomas, and this is CPR Classical’s Carol Countdown: The Festive Four. [Cue music — da-da-dun, da-da-dun.] Vote in our interactive bracket for Round 4 to help decide which carols advance and get entered to win a family four-pack of tickets to the Colorado Symphony’s “A Classical Christmas” on Dec. 5, at 7:30 p.m. See sweepstakes rules here . Fourth-round voting starts on Nov. 26 and is open until midnight Nov. 30. We’ll announce the carols that move on and open voting for Round 5 on Dec. 3. Voting will continue until we declare a champion on Tuesday, Dec. 8. Listen to CPR Classical’s Carol Countdown on Tuesday, Dec. 8, starting at 10 a.m., with the winner announced at 1 p.m. Listen for the Sound of the Season right after Thanksgiving on CPR Classical — your home for the holidays. Hear us in Denver at 88.1FM, listen online at CPRClassical.org , or tell your smart speaker to “Play CPR Classical.” “Carol Countdown” is a registered trademark of Colorado Public Radio.

title: Dress for Success offers women re-entering the workforce free business attire
summary: The non-profit provides donated clothes to women who've been away from the workforce, whether that be from incarceration or homelessness, and those facing financial barriers.
content: Belinda had been out of the workforce for about seven years because she was fighting an addiction, but she recently found a job. Earlier this month, she went to a 5,000-square-foot clothing warehouse in University Hills Plaza and came out with fresh gear to wear for her new position. And she didn’t spend a dime. Dress for Success , an international non-profit with a center in South Denver, provides free clothing that will help women slip seamlessly back into the workforce. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Dress for Success Denver’s showroom of lightly used women’s clothing in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026. Ad: “She actually was in a drug and alcohol treatment facility,” said the Colorado chapter CEO, Amara Martin. “She was just released after completing the program, and she is in transitional housing. Her case manager brought her down because she [was] starting a job on [a] Monday, and she’s very nervous because she hasn’t needed clothes. She felt like she didn’t look the part. She felt like she looked like what she had been through,” she said. Courtesy: Amara Martin Amara Martin, CEO of Dress For Success Denver, which has been open for about 20 years. That changed within a few hours. “Our personal stylist volunteers put her in some beautiful items: a gorgeous black pencil skirt, a black kitten heel, a little red jacket and she got a lovely scarf to go with it as well as a piece of jewelry,” Martin said. Belinda is one of about 250 women served by Dress for Success every month by Martin and about 60 volunteers. The organization is celebrating its 20th year in Colorado. The clothes come from the community. On the second Saturday of each month, people with women’s business clothes in good condition who want to donate them pack their vehicles with the garments, drive up to the building, and within 10 minutes, volunteers come to the car and unload the clothes. About 150 cars show up each month, Martin said. Elaine Tassy/CPR News Volunteers unload donations at Dress For Success Denver’s headquarters in the city’s University Hills neighborhood. Nov. 14, 2026. Dress for Success serves women who are returning to the workforce after a time away. That could be because of incarceration, homelessness, drug dependency or recently graduating from college or an educational program, Martin said. During the week, people like Belinda can come in and, depending on what they have lined up work-wise, can pick up different amounts of clothing. “If you are coming for an interview, you receive six pieces of clothing, one pair of shoes, one handbag, one wallet, five accessories, and three toiletry items,” Martin said. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Shoes fill racks inside Dress for Success Denver’s showroom of lightly used women’s clothing in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026. Those who are a little farther along in the job-reentry process can get even more: “You have an internship or a temporary position; that is nine pieces of clothing, one pair of shoes, one wallet, one handbag, five accessories, and three toiletry items. And then if you’re here [because you’ve gained] employment … you get 12 pieces of clothing, two pairs of shoes, wallets, handbags, five accessories, and five toiletry items at absolutely no cost,” Martin said. Most people find out about the program through other community-based organizations. “Workforce centers, shelters, community corrections [and] schools have us listed as one of their partners. We have about 180 organizations that we are working with in the Denver Metro area,” she said. The next donation date is Saturday, Dec. 12 from 10 a.m. until 2 p.m., and Martin said they’re especially in need of clothes sizes 16 and larger. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Dress for Success Denver’s headquarters in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026.

title: Black woman sues Denver Police after being accused of stealing a package that wasn’t stolen
summary: Officers accused Ebony Watson of stealing a laptop that had been in a mailroom the whole time.
content: Last March, three Denver police officers knocked on Ebony Watson’s door in the Lowry North Apartment Homes in the 8000 block of East 11th Ave in Denver. They accused Watson, a Black 49-year-old mother of two living with a disability, of having “taken other people’s packages” from the mail room earlier that day, March 3. Watson, dressed in a brown body suit, socks and slippers, opened the door and, standing outside of her apartment, calmly explained to the officers that she’d been in the mailroom the previous day to get a package — some soil for her houseplants — but didn’t know anything about a theft of a package that day. She offered to show them the soil package she’d picked up the day before, but they didn’t want to see it. She asked to see a video from the mailroom from which the package appeared to have gone missing, which one officer said he had in his possession, but was told no. Instead, the officers told her she knew why they were there, accused her of having purloined the box — later described as a laptop valued at 54 dollars — and then they locked her wrists in handcuffs and put her in the back of a police vehicle, according to multiple reports. In a video shot by the officers’ body-worn cameras and aired on 9News, she can be heard saying, “Oh my God! Are you guys serious?” and seen shakily taking a seat in the back of the police car, looking agitated and frightened. The officers kept her in the police car for more than 20 minutes as she heard her 8-year-old son screaming after he saw what had happened. Now, she’s fighting back. Last week, she filed a 14-page civil complaint against the three officers — Cory Stuper, Anthony Cochran, and Alec Olguin — alleging they discriminated against her because of her race; that they failed to intervene by doing any additional research that would have led them to know they had the wrong person; and that they unreasonably seized her from her home. The officers are expected to respond in about two weeks. Through her attorney Benjamin DeGolia , she in the suit requests a jury trial and financial damages as well as payment of her legal bills associated with the detainment, which sent her to her counselor for emotional support and new anxiety medication, and to her doctor who diagnosed her with bilateral wrist pain and swelling and bruising of her left wrist, according to the complaint. “These officers knew they had the wrong suspect. Ms. Watson looks nothing like the woman they suspected of stealing packages, who had long, red dreadlocks in the surveillance video,” DeGolia told CPR in an emailed statement. “Instead of performing even basic investigative tasks, they decided it was easier to just detain the first Black woman they came into contact with. They also could have easily shown Ms. Watson the surveillance video. Had they shown it to her as she requested, she may have been able to educate these white officers that not all Black women look the same. If our police departments want our communities to trust them, they need to do better,” DeGolia said in the same emailed statement. Watson’s complaint, filed in Denver County District Court on November 20, notes that on March 3, the day of the detainment, there was an apparent misunderstanding regarding the package, which had been reported stolen in a 911 call to the police. The parcel was found within a few days, in the very mailroom from which Watson had been accused of taking it from. The concept of Watson being the victim of mistaken identity stems from a video shown to police of another Black woman who was seen on the mailroom surveillance camera picking up a few packages. She had dyed red hair or extensions worn dreadlock-style in a ponytail at the top of her head. While both Watson and the woman in the video are Black, they have different hair colors (Watson’s is salt-and-pepper) and the woman in the video also appears to be slightly smaller and younger than Watson. Based on the police cam video, it appears police felt confident Watson was the woman in the video seen leaving the mailroom with several packages. The woman in the video was a red herring, DeGolia said in an email. “Police never made contact with her. No package was ever found to have been stolen, so I think it’s a fair assumption she was collecting her own packages.” Watson was released from the police car after officers felt apparently unable to confirm that Watson was the woman in the video, based on different hair color and other factors. She is seen being comforted by her 18-year-old daughter upon her release from the police vehicle. Whoever had gone into the mailroom to pick up a package – be it Watson or the red-haired woman – turned out not to matter anyway, because the package later turned up, neither missing nor stolen. “On March 5, 2026, management conducted a ‘full audit’ of the mailroom and found the laptop package underneath a few others … and management provided it to its owner,” per the complaint, which also states that once the package was found, “the Denver Police Department closed the case because ‘there was no crime committed.’” The next step will be a response to the complaint from the three officers. In a follow-up email, DeGolia explained that the officers have three weeks to respond to the complaint and will be represented by the DPD. “The officers are being sued as DPD officers, but under Colorado’s Enhance Law Enforcement Integrity Act, they’re sued individually. Absent rare circumstances, the City is required to indemnify the officers and will provide their legal defense,” he stated. “They have 21 days to file a responsive pleading, so their current deadline is 12/11.”

title: Why higher oil prices haven’t lifted Colorado production
summary: While the war with Iran has driven global oil prices higher, that has not yet translated into more oil production in Colorado.
content: While the war with Iran has driven global oil prices higher, that has not yet translated into more oil production in Colorado. The global supply decrease that began earlier this year has pushed oil above $100 a barrel at times. From March to August, U.S. crude oil production rose 1.7%, while Colorado’s fell 1.7%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The reason: the amount of time and money required to expand production makes short-term disruptions an unprofitable basis for ramping up drilling or pumping. “Our investment decisions are based on long-term competitiveness rather than short-term commodity price movements,” Kim McHugh, a vice president of Chevron, said in a statement. Occidental Petroleum told investors in August that it was shifting some drilling from Colorado’s Denver-Julesburg Basin to Wyoming’s Powder River Basin, where its wells were outperforming the basin average. The Colorado Oil and Gas Association said state permitting timelines help explain why drillers haven’t responded more quickly to higher prices. “It is very, very difficult for Colorado to respond in real time to current market conditions because of our permitting timelines,” said Lynn Granger, the president of COGA. The Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission said the median time from submission of an oil and gas development plan to a commission decision was 236 days. The agency said that as of Nov. 19, operators had state approval to drill 655 oil and gas wells across Colorado. It attributed recent shifts in rig counts and well starts to more efficient drilling and the maturity of the Denver-Julesburg Basin. What companies are doing Trisha Curtis, CEO of the energy analysis firm PetroNerds, said large publicly traded companies like Chevron and Occidental Petroleum now dominate drilling in Colorado because they have the resources to navigate onerous state regulations. “Smaller operators absolutely would’ve, day one, they would’ve said, ‘Let’s increase output,’” said Curtis. Large operators, however, tend to be more cautious, even if they have permits approved to drill more. “They’re not going to drill through those permits just because they have a few months of high oil prices,” said Curtis. “They’re going to have a very steady as you go plan.” Ian Lange, an economics professor at the Colorado School of Mines, said that Colorado’s regulations may favor large operators, but that doesn’t necessarily explain lower production. He said North Dakota provides a useful comparison to Colorado in terms of production. From March to August, North Dakota’s oil production rose 3.4%. In August, North Dakota’s oil production was still 23% below its 2019 monthly peak, and Colorado’s was 21% below its own, according to EIA data. “Whatever you want to say about North Dakota, I’m guessing you’re not going to claim they have the same environmental regulations as Colorado,” said Lange. In Colorado, “if they want to drill some more, they can drill some more,” said Lange. Aaron Weiss, executive director of the Center for Western Priorities, an environmental group, called the idea that Colorado’s regulations explain the sluggish production “nonsense.” He pointed to what oil executives tell investors about keeping spending in check and returning money to shareholders. “At the end of the day, it’s about protecting neighborhoods, protecting families, protecting public health,” Weiss said. “There’s nothing in these regulations that’s actually slowing production. It is entirely a choice that these oil and gas producers are making.”

title: ‘Plastic Shaman’ author Annette McGivney on trust, cultural appropriation and the search for wellness
summary: Cortez journalist Annette McGivney’s book, “Plastic Shaman,” examines the 2009 self-help retreat near Sedona, Arizona, that led to the deaths of James Shore, Kirby Brown and Liz Neuman.
content: The wellness industry’s promises of healing can come at a cost. In her new book, “Plastic Shaman”, Cortez journalist Annette McGivney investigates a 2009 self-help retreat that left three people dead following the exploitation of Indigenous spirituality. She spoke with CPR’s Hayley Sanchez. This interview has been excerpted for length. Questions and answers retain their original wording. Hayley Sanchez: Who was James Arthur Ray and what were people hoping he could offer them when they signed up for his retreats? Annette McGivney : James Arthur Ray was a very famous self-help guru from about 2006 to 2009. And he wrote this book that was on the New York Times bestseller list called “Harmonic Wealth” that made the promise that you can earn a lot of money and also become spiritually enlightened at the same time. And so people really bought into that idea. Sanchez: How did you confront your own biases and your own appropriation in the wellness industry? McGivney : This book is not just a judgmental thing. It’s not trying to shame people who are into new age self-help and maybe get deceived by some people because I am transparent with the reader in saying I too have been interested in new age self-help over the years. And as a survivor of a home when I was a child that was very violent, I grew up in a domestic violence situation. And as an adult, I definitely sought healing from that trauma in these people. It kind of made me aware of my idea around wellness is no longer so focused on myself. It’s more focused on the broader community. If the community is well, I’m healthier as well. It’s not just about me. Hayley Sanchez/CPR News Author Annette McGivney and her book, “Plastic Shaman.” Durango, Colo. Oct. 1, 2026. Sanchez: As a white journalist writing about the exploitation of Indigenous cultures, did you ever grapple with, ‘Am I the right person to tell the story?’ or did you feel any guilt while writing? McGivney : I absolutely feel guilt and shame about what Indigenous people have experienced, that I have benefited from this settler colonial culture that has been created, that my father and grandfather and great-grandfather, who immigrated from Ireland, we’ve all benefited from it. In that way, I feel a responsibility to try and repair harms or atone in any way I can, which is through my journalism. I guess I’m an advocate in that way, but I am not trying to speak for Indigenous people. I am very careful in the book to let them speak. I just say what they told me. I’m not speaking for Indigenous people. I’m just sharing what they have shared with me, and they’ve shared it with me because I am a white person and I’m talking to white people. So this book, I mean, it’s wonderful if Native Americans like to read it, but this is for white people. Sanchez: Talk about that healing ceremony that came many years later between the family of one of the victims, James Shore, and Indigenous folks who prayed for the family for years. What was it like to witness? McGivney : It was something that the leader, Lance Morris, had consulted with tribal elders about and saying, “I want to do this, but we’re not going to do any kind of ritual that should only be done by Native Americans.” It was planned in a way that was appropriate for non-Native people to participate in. And there (are) plenty of examples of that. It doesn’t mean that as a white person that you need to be totally cut off from Native culture, but you just need to be involved with their permission, with protocols that they allow. It was just realizing how much this group of Native Americans cared about what happened and how sad they were that James Shore had been killed and that the others had been killed. It meant a lot, and it helped the Native participants also. It helped them to see that James Shore’s family, that the kids were doing okay.

And so people really bought into that idea. Sanchez: How did you confront your own biases and your own appropriation in the wellness industry? McGivney : This book is not just a judgmental thing. It’s not trying to shame people who are into new age self-help and maybe get deceived by some people because I am transparent with the reader in saying I too have been interested in new age self-help over the years. And as a survivor of a home when I was a child that was very violent, I grew up in a domestic violence situation. And as an adult, I definitely sought healing from that trauma in these people. It kind of made me aware of my idea around wellness is no longer so focused on myself. It’s more focused on the broader community. If the community is well, I’m healthier as well. It’s not just about me. Hayley Sanchez/CPR News Author Annette McGivney and her book, “Plastic Shaman.” Durango, Colo. Oct. 1, 2026. Sanchez: As a white journalist writing about the exploitation of Indigenous cultures, did you ever grapple with, ‘Am I the right person to tell the story?’ or did you feel any guilt while writing? McGivney : I absolutely feel guilt and shame about what Indigenous people have experienced, that I have benefited from this settler colonial culture that has been created, that my father and grandfather and great-grandfather, who immigrated from Ireland, we’ve all benefited from it. In that way, I feel a responsibility to try and repair harms or atone in any way I can, which is through my journalism. I guess I’m an advocate in that way, but I am not trying to speak for Indigenous people. I am very careful in the book to let them speak. I just say what they told me. I’m not speaking for Indigenous people. I’m just sharing what they have shared with me, and they’ve shared it with me because I am a white person and I’m talking to white people. So this book, I mean, it’s wonderful if Native Americans like to read it, but this is for white people. Sanchez: Talk about that healing ceremony that came many years later between the family of one of the victims, James Shore, and Indigenous folks who prayed for the family for years. What was it like to witness? McGivney : It was something that the leader, Lance Morris, had consulted with tribal elders about and saying, “I want to do this, but we’re not going to do any kind of ritual that should only be done by Native Americans.” It was planned in a way that was appropriate for non-Native people to participate in. And there (are) plenty of examples of that. It doesn’t mean that as a white person that you need to be totally cut off from Native culture, but you just need to be involved with their permission, with protocols that they allow. It was just realizing how much this group of Native Americans cared about what happened and how sad they were that James Shore had been killed and that the others had been killed. It meant a lot, and it helped the Native participants also. It helped them to see that James Shore’s family, that the kids were doing okay.

title: Signs of another high-stakes legislative showdown brewing over statewide tobacco rules
summary: Gov.-elect Phil Weiser signaled support for a statewide proposal during a fight last year over a ban on the sales of flavored tobacco in Denver.
content: Come January, Colorado will swear in a new Democratic governor and a new Democratic supermajority in the General Assembly. And the two sides that frequently face off over rules governing tobacco and nicotine sales appear to be gearing up to renew their fight during the next legislative session. The president of the Rocky Mountain Smoke Free Alliance, a coalition of independent retailers and manufacturers of vape, nicotine and tobacco products, told journalists at the state Capitol on Nov. 18 his group supports several ideas aimed at limiting sales to underage Coloradans. “We’re hoping to fix the problems that are in the market,” said John-Paul Willett, who operates Red Star Vapor. He said it has retail and manufacturing facilities in five states, with 39 stores and 140 employees in Colorado. “We do have retailers who aren’t strictly IDing people, and aren’t conducting age verification vigorously in retail stores. We want to solve that problem.” He said he anticipates anti-tobacco groups will pursue a statewide ban on the sales of flavored tobacco, like the ones that lawmakers turned down in 2022 and 2024 . In 2022, a bill to ban the sale of flavored tobacco statewide failed after Democratic Gov. Jared Polis said the issue should be handled at the local level. “My hope is that we can have these conversations and come to reasonable solutions where we’re not staring down the barrel of statewide flavor bans,” Willett told CPR. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser signaled support for a statewide proposal during a fight last year over a ban on the sales of flavored tobacco in Denver, which voters ultimately approved. Willett said the proposal from businesses that sell tobacco and nicotine products would include several provisions, like increasing fines and penalties for retailers that get caught selling nicotine products to minors and removing products from the market that directly appeal to minors. Those include ones that have built-in video games, are disguised as office products or school products, or have decorations or animations that target children. He said the group also backs language that would give law enforcement the tools they need to crack down on online sales. “You have a lot of out-of-state online retailers that aren’t age gating (verifying the age of a buyer) and are selling into Colorado,” Willett said. Kevin J. Beaty/CPR News A rack of nicotine products is completely empty in a central Denver 7-Eleven. Oct. 23, 2026. The trade group also proposes adding nicotine products like vapes or nicotine pouches to the Colorado Tobacco Manufacturer’s Certification Directory, which he said would give the state more oversight of products on the market. He said the legislation is being drafted with Sen. Tom Sullivan, a Democrat from Centennial. “Protecting Colorado kids means holding accountable the businesses that break the law and the manufacturers that put products designed to attract children on the market,” said Sullivan, via email. He said the proposal would increase transparency and make sure businesses play by the rules. Reaction from an anti-tobacco advocate “If Colorado is serious about protecting the health of our kids, the policy to do exactly that is to end the sale of all flavored tobacco products,” said Jodi Radke, regional director of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids , via email. That group and other anti-tobacco advocates have long argued the vast majority of adults who use tobacco started before turning 21 and most kids who try it use flavored products like vapes and oral nicotine pouches, like Zyn, whose popularity has grown rapidly. She said stricter regulations and increased fines essentially respond to the symptom of the problem, noting more than 420 municipalities nationally, including 15 in Colorado , like Denver, Boulder and Glenwood Springs, have approved a policy that ends the sale of flavored tobacco. Earlier this month, community leaders in Aurora announced a similar campaign in Colorado’s third-largest city. John Daley/CPR News Jodi Radke, regional director of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, attends an event pushing to ban the sales of flavored tobacco in Aurora. Oct. 29, 2026. “Kids do not purchase their products over the internet,” Radke said, citing the most recent state data . “Only 6% do so, compared to nearly 30% who access tobacco products via a peer or friend, notably, and most commonly, a social source, of age. Around 13% purchase directly from a store.” Radke also said product registries and certification, passed in other states, have not been successful, “and only lead our elected officials down a rabbit hole, creating a mirage that this will directly impact use rates amongst our kids. It will not.” Colorado data Ten percent of Colorado youth vaped in the last month, according to the latest survey data , released earlier this year. That was up from 9% in 2023. Among high school students, the survey found 3.4% of them used oral nicotine pouches in the past 30 days. About half that percentage of middle schoolers said they’d ever used oral nicotine pouches. Products like Zyn, whose sales have skyrocketed, are so new, it’s the first time the state has asked about it. The survey found among high school students who report current vaping, nine in 10 used flavored vapes. For those using oral nicotine pouches, eight in 10 used flavored products. Among those smoking, 28% smoked flavored cigarettes. A smaller statewide survey found a rising and higher percentage of young people using e-cigarettes. It said 22% of teens reported vaping in the last 30 days.

title: As shop owners face new challenges, they hope Small Business Saturday will boost local support
summary: Colorado small business owners say the annual shopping day, which started in the Great Recession, is as much about building community as it is about supporting local shops.
content: For Morgan Calderini, Small Business Saturday is about sending the message that independent brick-and-mortar shops are no longer just places to buy things. They’re also places where people can gather, learn something new and connect with others. “In this whole sea of buy, buy, buy, support a small business, we just invite people to come down and maybe make something,” Calderini, owner of Ladyfingers Letterpress in Colorado Springs, told CPR News. “Or pick out a card to send to a loved one.” The annual shopping day encourages consumers to support independent businesses. It began more than 15 years ago, when American Express launched the campaign in the wake of the 2008 recession. Ad: “The origin of it is pretty corporate,” Calderini acknowledged. “So, I think it’s an opportunity to think about how we support and where we support.” “For us, Small Business Saturday is really a chance to extend our gratitude to our customers,” she said. Ladyfingers Letterpress is leaning into that idea this year with two drop-in workshops focused on candle-making and journal-making. Courtesy: Morgan Calderini Morgan Calderini holds a coupon from her store, Ladyfingers Letterpress, in Colorado Springs. They will be handed out on Small Business Saturday. At Tangled Ball Yarn in Edgewater, owner Marsha Corn hopes to see a steady stream of customers come through the door Saturday, but she also hopes to give them a place to gather and make their own gifts. “We’ll probably have people hanging out in the store, because people are always hanging out at my tables to knit or crochet, socialize,” she said. “That’s what my store is about.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News Marsha Corn, owner of The Tangled Ball in Edgewater Public Market, shows a knitting kit they will sell during Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026. Corn has prepared displays of gift ideas to encourage customers to explore the possibilities of crafting, whether they’re making something for themselves or creating a gift for someone else. “It’s good for our souls to craft and make things, to get out of our mind and concentrate on the task at hand instead of everything else going on,” she said. Calderini says the day is also about local businesses supporting each other. McKenzie Lange/CPR News Yarn on sale at The Tangled Ball, which will participate in Small Business Saturday, in Edgewater Public Market. Nov. 25, 2026. Ladyfingers is partnering with other local businesses through a holiday coupon book, which features specials from participating businesses, like a free card with purchases over $6 or a free lavender lemonade at a local restaurant with the purchase of six cards. Meanwhile, Little Blue Pigeon Books in Denver is partnering with four other downtown bookstores on a literary passport program encouraging shoppers to visit each location. “I think small businesses, and especially mine, survive because we support our community, and our community does that for us too,” Paige Dungan, who recently opened the book shop, said. “I truly believe that (we) — especially independent bookstores — offer a space for everyone to feel seen, wanted, and connected either with a story or a person.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News A passerby walks past Little Blue Pigeon Books in Larimer Square. Nov. 25, 2026. Dungan hopes the program will help people explore and introduce them to the independent businesses that make their towns unique. Still, in an era of new economic challenges, the financial upside of the shopping holiday continues to hold value to store owners. Corn said Small Business Saturday accounted for a significant share of Tangled Ball Yarn’s holiday shopping weekend revenue. McKenzie Lange/CPR News A map of bookstores inside Little Blue Pigeon Books in Larimer Square shows a map of stores participating in a literary passport book for Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026. “Most of my business will be on Small Business Saturday in the next three days,” she said. “So last year we did, probably 25% to 30% more on Small Business Saturday than we did on Black Friday.” For Megan Alfaro on the Western Slope, Small Business Saturday is the biggest sales day of the year at her store, Colorado Baby. “It’s a really fun day,” she said. “I love Small Business Saturday because you don’t have to entice people to come in.” Stina Sieg/CPR News Megan Alfaro, owner of Colorado Baby, stands for a portrait inside the store in downtown Grand Junction. Alfaro says Small Business Saturday is her busiest day of the year. One of the things she appreciates most is customers coming in because they want to support independent businesses, rather than looking for a discount. Even with the financial reality, Dungan said she doesn’t set sales goals for the day because money isn’t her sole mission. “What I like to say is Small Business Saturday is about humans really getting to know one another and connecting by heart first and product second,” she said. “Hopefully it’s a reminder that small business is out here, that not everything needs to be bought online or by a big box store,” Corn said. “We’re doing fine financially. We’re okay. So what it is, for me, is the continuation of building a community, supporting a community, creating friendships. That’s what the day is about.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News People shop at Edgewater Public Market ahead of Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026.

title: How a Western Slope wildlife nonprofit became a baby bear orphanage
summary: Following brutal drought, a foundation in Silt has taken in more than 30 bear cubs.
content: It’s been a hard year to be a bear in Colorado. A spring freeze, combined with drought and wildfires in the warmer months, has stressed out American black bears, forcing them to lumber farther into human civilization in search of food. As a result, there’s been a spike in bear emergency calls, conflicts and attacks — and a rash of baby bears orphaned or abandoned by their moms. A wildlife rehabilitation center in Silt usually cares for about five to 10 bear cubs a year. This year, it’s helped more than 30. “The bears have run amok,” said Nanci Limbach, the founder and executive director of the Pauline S. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation , a nonprofit named after her grandmother. Here are excerpts from her recent conversation with CPR News. Ad: What’s going on with these bears? Times got tough for Colorado bears pretty much from the moment they started to emerge from hibernation this spring. A hard freeze in mid-April “killed all the berries and all of the acorns that the bears would normally be eating,” Limbach said. The deep summer drought, which followed historically low snowpack, made things even worse, with some waterways completely drying up. Plus, large wildfires plagued the state this summer, driving bears from their normal habitat. Courtesy: Colorado Parks and Wildlife Colorado wildlife officials are cautioning residents to secure not just their trash and food this Halloween season but also their jack-o-lanterns. Bears consume 20,000 calories a day as they head into hibernation. It didn’t take long before they were wandering into populated areas in search of food, even breaking into houses and tents. “If you have low blood sugar, how grumpy are you? Well, I’m pretty sure that’s probably how those bears are feeling too, and you’re taking up their food source and their space,” Limbach said. She added that the fact that humans keep moving into bear habitat only makes the problem worse. Courtesy: Colorado Parks and Wildlife Colorado wildlife officials are cautioning residents to secure not just their trash and food this Halloween season but also their jack-o-lanterns. Bears consume 20,000 calories a day as they head into hibernation. Bustling with baby bears Bear cubs have been especially vulnerable to this year’s challenges — and can’t always rely on their mothers for help. In fact, when times are especially lean, Limbach explained that some moms practice “survival of the fittest” and actually abandon their offspring before heading into hibernation. “If she’s having trouble surviving herself, she needs to not care about a baby,” she explained. It’s a “hard thing and a sad thing” to see, Limbach said. It’s also part of how her organization ended up caring for more than 30 cubs, though some of those were orphaned or injured. Courtesy: Pauline S. Schneegas W The Pauline S. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation, in Silt, is caring for more than 30 bear cubs as winter sets in. The organization has seen an increase in bears due to a lack of forage in their habitat and the drought. Limbach said that some criticize her foundation’s work, saying they should “let nature take its course.” Limbach rejects that idea. Her organization is the only private nonprofit caring for bears in Colorado, though CPW has its own facility in the San Luis Valley. (It has also seen a big increase in baby bears this year.) In addition to the drought, they’ve cared for a lot of cubs whose mothers were hit by cars. “That isn’t nature. A human did that. There’s been people illegally shooting the mothers and that’s not nature, either,” Limbach said. “I think I just try to give back to the bears to try to get some balance back for them, despite what humans are doing to interfere with their lives.” She stressed that bears can be “good moms” during a normal year, but in years like this, they are forced to cut their losses, one bear cub at a time. “Mom needs to be able to make it back to the den so that she can have more babies,” Limbach said. What it takes to care for bears Limbach’s organization cares for all manner of wild animals, but with the influx of cubs this year, much of their work has been dedicated to keeping them safe, fed — and still wild. She and the organization’s few employees try to keep total separation between them and the bears, to shield them from imprinting on humans. “We spend very little time with them. That’s the whole point. You don’t want them being used to people,” she said. But she does want the bears to feel comfort. Stuffed bears donated by the public can help. Stina Sieg/CPR News Nanci Limbach, who founded the Pauline S. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation decades ago, takes pains to keep the bears (and other wildlife in her organization’s care) from being exposed to humans. She’ll often give them donated stuffed bears to play with and cuddle, though she’s unsure if they’ll go for this pink one. Silt, Nov. 11, 2026. “We put them in with the little cubs, and they just nestle up against them,” Limbach said. “It definitely calms them down.” The bears live in enclosures encased with privacy screens, grouped with other bears from their region of Colorado — a buddy for playing and roughhousing. Limbach likes to watch on game cameras set up in the enclosures. “We’ve had two sit in a bathtub one time, and they splashed each other like two little brothers, and it was the cutest darn thing,” she said. It’s the bears’ job to gain strength and weight, and these creatures take it seriously. Earlier this fall, “we were going through almost 2,000 pounds of fruit a week and probably about a thousand pounds of other food sources, as well,” Limbach said. Those additional foods include nuts and high-quality dog food (full of real meat and without by-products). This hefty mix meets bears’ nutritional needs. Much of this food is donated — her organization runs on donations and grants. While it takes in animals brought to them by Colorado Parks and Wildlife, it does not receive any state funding. Some of the bears the facility is caring for are too little to hibernate and will live through the winter in their enclosures. The sturdiest ones will be released into the wild during winter. They’ll already be in hibernation at the center when volunteers give them “a nice snowmobile ride” into the mountains, Limbach said. “We’ll have built a snow cave, and we’ll put them in there, and they’ll end up just coming out in March and April like all other bears.” Limbach explained that they seem to do well with this transition. “We’ve never had one go attack a person,” she said. “We’ve never had them get into trouble.” A love of bears Limbach cares for many species at her center, but she may be best known for helping bears. She’s fascinated by the creatures, especially their ability to delay when they give birth. Though a bear might breed sometime in the summer, she’ll almost always have her cub or cubs in January (or sometimes February). Basically, a ball of cells just waits for the right time to become life. “I mean, it just floats around the uterus and doesn’t do anything,” Limbach said. “And then eventually when she implants it, the fact that it totally develops within two months is just amazing.” In fact, the bear’s body decides how many cubs to have, perhaps based on what current conditions can allow. Limbach is not an overly sentimental person, but talks with admiration about the bear interactions she’s witnessed. She described one bear mother who was captured without her three cubs. McKenzie Lange/CPR News A mother bear and cub rest in a tree in the Harvey Park neighborhood of Denver on Aug. 18, 2026. At Limbach’s facility, she settled into an old fruit tree “and just cried, and it was the saddest thing,” she said. “We all felt so sorry for her.” When the bear was finally reunited with her cubs, she initially dunked and slammed them into the ground before finally putting her paws around them, embracing and nursing them. Limbach and her colleagues were in awe. “That was kind of like the mother who lost their kid in a mall: ‘Where have you been? Don’t you ever do that again, but I love you.’” When asked if she worries for the bears, she said yes — in this stressful year and the decades to come. Limbach worries about Colorado becoming even more developed, with more bear habitat being encroached upon by humans. “It’s just sad to think what the future will hold for any of the wild animals at that rate,” she said. It’s like a bumper sticker Limbach found at an antique store: “Save the bears. If you can’t live with them, you move.”

This year, it’s helped more than 30. “The bears have run amok,” said Nanci Limbach, the founder and executive director of the Pauline S. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation , a nonprofit named after her grandmother. Here are excerpts from her recent conversation with CPR News. Ad: What’s going on with these bears? Times got tough for Colorado bears pretty much from the moment they started to emerge from hibernation this spring. A hard freeze in mid-April “killed all the berries and all of the acorns that the bears would normally be eating,” Limbach said. The deep summer drought, which followed historically low snowpack, made things even worse, with some waterways completely drying up. Plus, large wildfires plagued the state this summer, driving bears from their normal habitat. Courtesy: Colorado Parks and Wildlife Colorado wildlife officials are cautioning residents to secure not just their trash and food this Halloween season but also their jack-o-lanterns. Bears consume 20,000 calories a day as they head into hibernation. It didn’t take long before they were wandering into populated areas in search of food, even breaking into houses and tents. “If you have low blood sugar, how grumpy are you? Well, I’m pretty sure that’s probably how those bears are feeling too, and you’re taking up their food source and their space,” Limbach said. She added that the fact that humans keep moving into bear habitat only makes the problem worse. Bustling with baby bears Bear cubs have been especially vulnerable to this year’s challenges — and can’t always rely on their mothers for help. In fact, when times are especially lean, Limbach explained that some moms practice “survival of the fittest” and actually abandon their offspring before heading into hibernation. “If she’s having trouble surviving herself, she needs to not care about a baby,” she explained. It’s a “hard thing and a sad thing” to see, Limbach said. It’s also part of how her organization ended up caring for more than 30 cubs, though some of those were orphaned or injured. Courtesy: Pauline S. Schneegas W The Pauline S. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation, in Silt, is caring for more than 30 bear cubs as winter sets in. The organization has seen an increase in bears due to a lack of forage in their habitat and the drought. Limbach said that some criticize her foundation’s work, saying they should “let nature take its course.” Limbach rejects that idea. Her organization is the only private nonprofit caring for bears in Colorado, though CPW has its own facility in the San Luis Valley. (It has also seen a big increase in baby bears this year.) In addition to the drought, they’ve cared for a lot of cubs whose mothers were hit by cars. “That isn’t nature. A human did that. There’s been people illegally shooting the mothers and that’s not nature, either,” Limbach said. “I think I just try to give back to the bears to try to get some balance back for them, despite what humans are doing to interfere with their lives.” She stressed that bears can be “good moms” during a normal year, but in years like this, they are forced to cut their losses, one bear cub at a time. “Mom needs to be able to make it back to the den so that she can have more babies,” Limbach said. What it takes to care for bears Limbach’s organization cares for all manner of wild animals, but with the influx of cubs this year, much of their work has been dedicated to keeping them safe, fed — and still wild. She and the organization’s few employees try to keep total separation between them and the bears, to shield them from imprinting on humans. “We spend very little time with them. That’s the whole point. You don’t want them being used to people,” she said. But she does want the bears to feel comfort. Stuffed bears donated by the public can help. Schneegas Wildlife Foundation decades ago, takes pains to keep the bears (and other wildlife in her organization’s care) from being exposed to humans. She’ll often give them donated stuffed bears to play with and cuddle, though she’s unsure if they’ll go for this pink one. Silt, Nov. 11, 2026. “We put them in with the little cubs, and they just nestle up against them,” Limbach said. “It definitely calms them down.” The bears live in enclosures encased with privacy screens, grouped with other bears from their region of Colorado — a buddy for playing and roughhousing. Limbach likes to watch on game cameras set up in the enclosures. “We’ve had two sit in a bathtub one time, and they splashed each other like two little brothers, and it was the cutest darn thing,” she said. It’s the bears’ job to gain strength and weight, and these creatures take it seriously. Earlier this fall, “we were going through almost 2,000 pounds of fruit a week and probably about a thousand pounds of other food sources, as well,” Limbach said. Those additional foods include nuts and high-quality dog food (full of real meat and without by-products). This hefty mix meets bears’ nutritional needs. Much of this food is donated — her organization runs on donations and grants. While it takes in animals brought to them by Colorado Parks and Wildlife, it does not receive any state funding. Some of the bears the facility is caring for are too little to hibernate and will live through the winter in their enclosures. The sturdiest ones will be released into the wild during winter. They’ll already be in hibernation at the center when volunteers give them “a nice snowmobile ride” into the mountains, Limbach said. “We’ll have built a snow cave, and we’ll put them in there, and they’ll end up just coming out in March and April like all other bears.” Limbach explained that they seem to do well with this transition. “We’ve never had one go attack a person,” she said. “We’ve never had them get into trouble.” A love of bears Limbach cares for many species at her center, but she may be best known for helping bears. She’s fascinated by the creatures, especially their ability to delay when they give birth. Though a bear might breed sometime in the summer, she’ll almost always have her cub or cubs in January (or sometimes February). Basically, a ball of cells just waits for the right time to become life. “I mean, it just floats around the uterus and doesn’t do anything,” Limbach said. “And then eventually when she implants it, the fact that it totally develops within two months is just amazing.” In fact, the bear’s body decides how many cubs to have, perhaps based on what current conditions can allow. Limbach is not an overly sentimental person, but talks with admiration about the bear interactions she’s witnessed. She described one bear mother who was captured without her three cubs. McKenzie Lange/CPR News A mother bear and cub rest in a tree in the Harvey Park neighborhood of Denver on Aug. 18, 2026. At Limbach’s facility, she settled into an old fruit tree “and just cried, and it was the saddest thing,” she said. “We all felt so sorry for her.” When the bear was finally reunited with her cubs, she initially dunked and slammed them into the ground before finally putting her paws around them, embracing and nursing them. Limbach and her colleagues were in awe. “That was kind of like the mother who lost their kid in a mall: ‘Where have you been? Don’t you ever do that again, but I love you.’” When asked if she worries for the bears, she said yes — in this stressful year and the decades to come. Limbach worries about Colorado becoming even more developed, with more bear habitat being encroached upon by humans. “It’s just sad to think what the future will hold for any of the wild animals at that rate,” she said. It’s like a bumper sticker Limbach found at an antique store: “Save the bears. If you can’t live with them, you move.”
